justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift from what I assessed as the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 266.5 was anchored heavily to the last observed price, with only a small expected move given typical daily volatility in the asset. For the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 268.0, reflecting a mild bullish lean based on recent momentum or trend signals while acknowledging that mean-reversion forces could easily offset any directional bias. At the one-month horizon, the estimate of 272.0 represents a continuation of that gentle upward trajectory, consistent with longer-term trend assumptions, though the conviction behind any single point estimate weakens considerably as the horizon extends.

The confidence interval widths were calibrated primarily to historical realized volatility. At one day, the interval of 257–276 is relatively tight, reflecting that most daily moves in a moderately volatile asset tend to cluster within a few percentage points of the prior close. By one week, the interval widens to 249–287, capturing the compounding uncertainty of multiple trading sessions and the possibility of a trending move in either direction. The one-month interval of 235–310 is substantially wider, acknowledging that over thirty or so trading days, macro shifts, sentiment changes, and compounding randomness can move prices meaningfully away from any starting anchor.

Several specific risks could push outcomes outside these stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in risk appetite — triggered by unexpected macroeconomic data, a central bank surprise, or a geopolitical shock — could produce a sharp selloff that breaks below 257 even within a single day, let alone over a month. On the upside, a strong catalyst such as a better-than-expected earnings report, a policy pivot, or a short-squeeze dynamic could drive prices well above 310 at the monthly horizon.

It is also worth noting that my intervals assume roughly continuous, liquid market conditions. If trading were halted, if liquidity dried up sharply, or if there were a structural break in the underlying fundamentals of the asset, realized outcomes could deviate far beyond what any historically grounded volatility model would predict. These tail scenarios are not fully captured in the stated 90% confidence intervals, which by construction exclude roughly 10% of plausible outcomes.
